title: Recover COVID Unemployment Fraud in Banks Act
official_title: To recover unclaimed pandemic-era unemployment compensation funds held by financial institutions or escheated to State unclaimed property administrators, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Beth Van Duyne (R-TX) and passed the House by voice vote (no recorded roll call); the bill directs recovery of improper pandemic unemployment payments and extends the related fraud statute of limitations to 10 years, and now awaits Senate consideration.
summary: Sets up a federal task force to find and get back pandemic unemployment money that was paid out improperly and is still sitting in banks or with state unclaimed-property offices. It also gives prosecutors more time to bring fraud cases tied to those pandemic unemployment programs.
brief: Creates a federal task force to recover improper pandemic unemployment payments held by banks and states, and extends the fraud statute of limitations to 10 years.

top_lines.headline: Pandemic Fund Recovery Task Force
subs: Task force convened within 30 days of enactment
Targets improper payments on prepaid debit cards held by banks or states
Labor Secretary reimburses states for related administrative costs

top_lines.headline: Fraud Statute of Limitations
subs: Extends the fraud prosecution deadline to 10 years
Covers PUA, FPUC/MEUC, and PEUC unemployment claims
Does not revive cases whose limitations period already expired

top_lines.headline: Coordination and Guidance
subs: National Recovery Coordinator designated by the Labor Secretary
Guidance issued to banks and state unclaimed-property offices
Model notice developed for identity-theft victims

items.main: Names the Act the "Recover COVID Unemployment Fraud in Banks Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — National Recovery Coordinator and Task Force

items.main: Directs the Secretary of Labor, in consultation with the Treasury Secretary, the Labor Department Inspector General, and the Attorney General, to designate a National Recovery Coordinator who convenes a "Recover Pandemic Unemployment Funds in Banks Task Force" not later than 30 days after enactment.
items.detail: The Task Force includes the Attorney General, the Secretary of Labor, the Labor Department Inspector General, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Chairman of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, or their designees. It coordinates with state agencies to identify federal pandemic unemployment payments issued on prepaid debit cards that are held by financial institutions or that were transferred to and are held by a state unclaimed-property agency.

items.main: Requires the Task Force to develop model recovery processes and issue guidance to state agencies, financial institutions, and state unclaimed-property administrators for returning improper payments to the appropriate state agency.
items.detail: Guidance to states covers reviewing whether a payment was improper, whether cost-effective recovery is possible (including a dollar threshold or a methodology for calculating one), and actions to take if fraud is determined. Guidance to banks is issued with the Comptroller of the Currency and the FDIC Chairman; guidance to unclaimed-property administrators is issued with the Treasury Secretary. The Task Force must consult states and incorporate best practices from prior state recovery attempts.

items.main: Requires the Secretary of Labor to reimburse states for all administrative costs incurred from coordinating with the Task Force by reason of an agreement under section 2102, 2104, or 2107 of the CARES Act.
items.detail: Defines "Federal pandemic unemployment compensation" as payments under CARES Act sections 2102(b), 2104(b)(1), and 2107(a)(2), and defines "improper payment" as any amount of a pandemic unemployment payment to which the individual is not entitled. State-law terms take the meanings in section 205 of the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970.

sections.label: Section 3 — Extension of the Statute of Limitations

items.main: Amends CARES Act sections 2102, 2104, and 2107 to require that any criminal prosecution or civil enforcement action for fraud tied to a claim funded in whole or in part by those pandemic unemployment programs be brought not later than 10 years after the violation or conspiracy.
items.detail: The 10-year period applies to violations of, or conspiracies to violate, sections 371, 641, 1028A, 1029, 1341, 1343, 1344, 1349, 1956, and 1957 of title 18 and sections 3729 and 3802 of title 31. It does not apply where the applicable statute of limitations already expired before the Act's enactment. The amendments take effect on the date of enactment.

underreported.summary: The 10-year limitations period does not apply to any prosecution or enforcement action whose applicable statute of limitations already expired before the Act's enactment.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned as an extension of the statute of limitations, but this carve-out means it does not revive cases that were already time-barred, limiting which claims the longer window can reach.

underreported.summary: The Secretary of Labor must reimburse states for all administrative costs incurred from coordinating with the Task Force under CARES Act sections 2102, 2104, or 2107.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is framed around recovering funds held by banks, but it also creates a federal reimbursement obligation to states for the administrative work of that coordination.

gaps: The bill directs recovery of improper payments held by banks and states but does not appropriate funds for the Task Force's own operating costs.
The bill defines "improper payment" as any amount to which the individual is not entitled but does not set the dollar threshold for cost-effective recovery, leaving it to Task Force guidance.
The bill requires guidance to identity-theft victims but does not specify a remedy or restitution process for individuals whose identities were fraudulently used.
The bill extends the fraud statute of limitations for individuals but does not address limitations periods for the financial institutions holding the funds.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Van Duyne
featured_quotes.text: This commonsense legislation creates a Federal task force to work with States to recover unspent Federal pandemic unemployment funds that remain frozen in financial institutions and return those taxpayer dollars to the U.S. Treasury, but Congress must act quickly. Last December, the Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General issued two fraud alerts identifying nearly $1 billion in unspent Federal unemployment funds frozen by banks because of suspected fraud.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Suozzi
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I yield myself the balance of my time. H.R. 8873, the Recover COVID Unemployment Fraud in Banks Act, is a commonsense bill that helps eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse; recovers stolen taxpayer dollars; and protects some of our most vulnerable citizens, including older Americans.

added: New National Recovery Coordinator position and Recover Pandemic Unemployment Funds in Banks Task Force, convened within 30 days of enactment
New requirement that the Secretary of Labor reimburse states for administrative costs of coordinating with the Task Force
modified: Amends CARES Act section 2102 (15 U.S.C. 9021) to add a 10-year statute of limitations for fraud tied to Pandemic Unemployment Assistance claims
Amends CARES Act section 2104 (15 U.S.C. 9023) to add a 10-year statute of limitations for fraud tied to Federal Pandemic Unemployment Compensation and Mixed Earner Unemployment Compensation claims
Amends CARES Act section 2107 (15 U.S.C. 9025) to add a 10-year statute of limitations for fraud tied to Pandemic Emergency Unemployment Compensation claims
